hagrid.idea: A lighthouse keeper realizes the light has been guiding something other than ships.
hagrid.script:
For thirty years, old Thomas kept the light burning to guide ships home. He never once wondered what else might be watching from the dark.

The storms came often on this coast, and Thomas knew every one by name. But the night the fog rolled in thick as wool, no ship's horn answered his beam. Only silence. And then... a sound. Not the creak of a hull. Something deeper. Something that breathed.

He climbed the tower stairs, lantern in hand, and swept the great light across the black water. That's when he saw them. Eyes. Dozens of them, rising just beneath the waves, drawn to the glow like moths to a candle. Not ships. Never ships.

For thirty years he thought he'd been saving sailors. But the log books told a different tale — vessels that vanished on the calmest nights, always when the light shone brightest. He hadn't been guiding boats to safety. He'd been calling something up from the deep, ringing a dinner bell across the sea.

Thomas reached for the switch. His hand trembled over the great lamp. Turn it off, and the ships would wreck on the rocks. Leave it on, and feed the hungry dark.

But it was already too late. Below him, the water began to rise. And the eyes... the eyes were climbing the stairs.

So if you ever sail a lonely coast and see a lighthouse burning bright — ask yourself who lit it. And what, exactly, it's meant to guide home.
